summary: The EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP) lets a peer re-authenticate efficiently with an ER server through a compatible authenticator. This document specifies Diameter support for ERP. It defines a new Diameter ERP application and new AVPs for carrying ERP messages and related cryptographic material.

plainLanguage.summary: Once you have shown your ID, signing back in later should be quicker. This explains how the network's account servers pass along that quick sign-in.

questions: what is the diameter erp application id
how does erp bootstrapping work in diameter
subtitle: How Diameter carries fast EAP re-authentication between an access network and a re-authentication server.

tldr.problem: Running a full EAP authentication every time a device moves or reconnects is slow. The EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP) offers a quicker one-round-trip exchange, but it needs a way to travel over Diameter and a way to get keys to the re-authentication server.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a new Diameter application, Diameter ERP (Application Id 13), that reuses the Diameter-EAP-Request and Diameter-EAP-Answer commands. It adds the ERP-RK-Request and ERP-Realm AVPs and uses the Key AVP to carry the root key and the re-authentication master session key.
tldr.outcome: With this in place, an authenticator can send an EAP-Initiate/Re-auth message to an ER server and get back an EAP-Finish/Re-auth message plus a fresh key. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 6942 is a Proposed Standard from May 2013, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds directly on RFC 6696 (ERP) and RFC 4072 (Diameter EAP).

sections.title: Introduction and Terminology
sections.content:
The EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP) is defined in RFC 6696. It has two steps. In bootstrapping, a root key is derived from the Extended Master Session Key (EMSK) created during EAP authentication and is transported from the EAP server to the ER (EAP Re-authentication) server. In re-authentication, the peer and the ER server do a one-round-trip exchange that results in mutual authentication. ERP adds two EAP codes for this, EAP-Initiate and EAP-Finish.

This RFC defines how Diameter transports the ERP messages. It defines a new Application Identifier for ERP and reuses the Diameter EAP commands Diameter-EAP-Request (DER) and Diameter-EAP-Answer (DEA) from RFC 4072. It also describes how the root key is handed out during bootstrapping.

The text writes ERP/DER and ERP/DEA for these commands when the Application Id is Diameter ERP, and EAP/DER and EAP/DEA when it is Diameter EAP. A root key (RK) means the re-authentication Root Key (rRK) or the re-authentication Domain-Specific Root Key (rDSRK), depending on whether the ER server is in the home domain or a foreign domain.
sections.plainLanguage: When you first log in, a long checking process happens. ERP is a shortcut for later visits, and this RFC says how the shortcut message is delivered between computers.

sections.title: Assumptions and Protocol Overview
sections.content:
The RFC assumes at most one logical ER server per domain. If several physical servers are used for robustness, a replication mechanism must keep the ERP state, such as root keys, in sync, but that mechanism is out of scope. It likewise assumes at most one EAP server in the home domain, and key management domain names are assumed to match Diameter realm names.

The parties are the peer, the authenticator, the ER server and the home EAP server. The ER server is either in the home domain (the same as the EAP server) or in the local domain (the same as the authenticator). When the peer starts an ERP exchange, the authenticator builds a DER message with the Diameter ERP Application Id. If a local ER server exists, Diameter routing MUST send the message there. Otherwise it is routed by the Destination-Realm AVP, taken from the realm part of the keyName-NAI.

If no ER server is reachable in the home domain either, the message cannot be delivered and a DIAMETER_UNABLE_TO_DELIVER error MUST be generated and returned to the authenticator. The authenticator MAY cache that result for a limited time, and MAY fall back to full EAP authentication.

An ER server that gets the message looks for a valid, unexpired root key matching the keyName part of the User-Name AVP. If it finds one, it processes the ERP message and answers with an ERP/DEA that includes the re-authentication Master Session Key (rMSK). If it lacks the key and the message has the 'B' (bootstrapping) flag set, it SHOULD act as a proxy and forward the request to the home EAP server with the ERP-RK-Request AVP added.
sections.plainLanguage: The message goes to the nearest helper who already knows you. If that helper does not know you yet, it asks your home office, and if nobody can be reached the guard just does the long check again.

sections.title: Bootstrapping the ER Server
sections.content:
The peer must derive the same keying material as the ER server, so it must learn the ER server's domain name. How it learns this is out of scope, though an authenticator might advertise it. The RFC covers two moments for bootstrapping.

Implicit bootstrapping happens during the initial EAP authentication. The ER server acts as a Diameter EAP proxy and adds an ERP-RK-Request AVP to the first DER. A home server that does not support ERP simply ignores the AVP. One that does saves the ERP-Realm value, and when authentication succeeds and the method produced an EMSK, it MUST derive the rRK as specified in RFC 6696 and return it in a Key AVP with Key-Type rRK. The ER server saves and removes that Key AVP and may add an ERP-Realm AVP so the authenticator can tell the peer which domain is bootstrapped. The upside is that the server is ready at once; the downside is wasted effort for peers that never use ERP.

Explicit bootstrapping happens during the first re-authentication and is only needed when there is no local ER server but there is one in the home domain. The home ER server receives an ERP/DER with the 'B' flag set, changes the Application Id to Diameter EAP, and forwards it with the ERP-RK-Request AVP to the home EAP server. That server answers with a Key AVP carrying the rRK, and the ER server restores the ERP Application Id and caches the key. This is less resource intensive, but the first re-authentication needs a round trip to the home EAP server.

If the home Diameter EAP server does not understand the ERP-specific EAP-Initiate code, it MUST send an EAP/DEA with a Permanent Failure Result-Code, for example DIAMETER_ERROR_EAP_CODE_UNKNOWN or DIAMETER_UNABLE_TO_COMPLY, and include a Failed-AVP containing a copy of the EAP-Payload AVP.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the shortcut works, the helper needs a copy of your special key. It can get it while you first sign in, or the first time you ask for the shortcut and it has to phone your home office.

sections.title: The Re-authentication Exchange
sections.content:
Once the ER server is bootstrapped, re-authentication takes one round trip. The peer sends an EAP-Initiate/Re-auth message through the authenticator. Alternatively the authenticator may first send an EAP-Initiate/Re-auth-Start message to prompt the peer. An authenticator that supports only plain Diameter EAP discards the unknown EAP-Initiate packet, and the peer should fall back to full EAP authentication.

The authenticator builds an ERP/DER. The Application Id in the header and the Auth-Application-Id AVP are both set to Diameter ERP (code 13). The keyName-NAI from the ERP message supplies the User-Name and Destination-Realm AVPs, and the EAP-Payload AVP carries the EAP-Initiate/Re-auth message.

The ER server answers with an ERP/DEA, again with Application Id and Auth-Application-Id set to Diameter ERP. The EAP-Payload AVP holds the EAP-Finish/Re-auth message, and if authentication succeeded, a Key AVP with the rMSK is included. The authenticator forwards the EAP-Payload to the peer and uses the Keying-Material AVP as a shared secret for a lower-layer secure association.
sections.plainLanguage: You show your shortcut pass, the helper checks it, and sends back an okay plus a new secret for this visit. That is just one question and one answer.

sections.title: Application Id, AVPs and Result Code
sections.content:
The new application is called Diameter ERP and has Application Id 13. An ER server MUST advertise it by including an Auth-Application-Id AVP with that value in its Capabilities-Exchange-Request and Capabilities-Exchange-Answer commands. The Application Id mainly ensures correct routing and that advertising nodes understand the new AVPs, even though those AVPs have the 'M' flag cleared.

Two new AVPs are defined, both with the 'M' and 'V' bits cleared. ERP-RK-Request (code 618) is a Grouped AVP the ER server uses to show it is willing to act as ER server for a session; it contains an ERP-Realm AVP. ERP-Realm (code 619) is of type DiameterIdentity and names the realm where the ER server sits.

The existing Key AVP from RFC 6734 carries keys. Key-Type MUST be 1 for rRK or 2 for rMSK. Keying-Material holds the rRK sent from the home EAP server to the ER server, or the rMSK sent from the ER server to the authenticator. Key-Name holds the EMSKname, and Key-Lifetime gives the lifetime in seconds and MUST NOT exceed the remaining lifetime of the EMSK. One new Permanent Failure Result-Code is defined: DIAMETER_ERROR_EAP_CODE_UNKNOWN (5048), which tells the peer that the EAP-Payload AVP held an EAP packet with an unknown EAP code.
sections.plainLanguage: This part is the list of new labels on the envelopes: one saying which office is helping, one naming the key, and one error note that says, I do not know that kind of message.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to the security considerations of RFC 4072, RFC 5295, RFC 6696, RFC 6733 and RFC 6734, which all apply.

Because the application carries sensitive data including cryptographic keys, it MUST be protected with TLS, DTLS or IPsec ESP. If TLS or DTLS is used, the negotiated bulk encryption algorithm MUST be non-null, and if ESP is used, the encryption algorithm MUST be non-null.
sections.plainLanguage: Because secret keys are passed around, the messages must travel in a locked box, never in an open envelope.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA allocated the Application Id "Diameter ERP" (code 13) in the "Application IDs" registry. It also allocated AVP codes for ERP-RK-Request (618) and ERP-Realm (619), and the Permanent Failure Result-Code value DIAMETER_ERROR_EAP_CODE_UNKNOWN (5048).
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of numbers got three new entries, so nobody else will use the same numbers for something different.
